theme: One voice wakes an environmental movement

then.title: Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring
then.hook: The book that warned pesticides like DDT were silencing birds and poisoning the food chain.
then.text: Biologist Rachel Carson published Silent Spring in September 1962, documenting how DDT and other pesticides harmed wildlife and could threaten people. The chemical industry attacked her, but the book became a bestseller and President Kennedy ordered a scientific review of pesticides.

now.title: Greta Thunberg’s School Strike
now.hook: Remember the Friday climate strikes: a lone Swedish teenager’s sign, then millions of students marching.
now.text: In August 2018, 15-year-old Greta Thunberg began skipping school to sit outside Sweden’s parliament with a sign reading “School strike for climate”. Students worldwide copied her as Fridays for Future. On 20 September 2019, organizers counted about 4 million strikers.

followed: Public pressure grew fast. About 20 million Americans joined the first Earth Day in 1970, the Environmental Protection Agency opened that year, and the US banned DDT for farm use in 1972.

next.title: A new voice for a new threat
next.text: Around 2074, a single voice might again rally millions, perhaps over microplastics in human bodies, failing oceans or a geoengineering project, spreading through media we cannot yet picture.
next.watch: Rising alarm over microplastics, ocean acidification or solar geoengineering, and young activists organizing across borders around one simple act.

breaks: DDT could be banned by national laws within a decade, while cutting greenhouse gases requires every major economy to change how it makes energy.

theme: Protests ripple across the globe at once

then.title: The global protest wave of 1968
then.hook: Barricades in Paris, Soviet tanks in Prague: the year the whole world seemed to boil over.
then.text: In May 1968, French students built barricades and about 10 million workers went on strike. Americans protested the Vietnam War, and riots followed Martin Luther King’s assassination. Soviet-led troops crushed the Prague Spring, and Mexican troops fired on students at Tlatelolco.

now.title: The George Floyd protests
now.hook: Remember June 2020: masked crowds kneeling in the streets in the middle of a pandemic.
now.text: A Minneapolis police officer killed George Floyd on 25 May 2020, kneeling on his neck for over nine minutes. Video of his death sparked protests in all 50 states and dozens of countries. Polls suggested 15 to 26 million Americans took part.

followed: Elections swung toward order. Richard Nixon won the US presidency promising “law and order”, de Gaulle’s party won a landslide in June, and Prague’s reforms were rolled back under Soviet pressure.

next.title: Global protests sparked within hours
next.text: Around 2072, one video or one killing might again set off protests in dozens of countries within days, organized on networks that do not yet exist.
next.watch: Large generations of young people with blocked prospects, a shared grievance that crosses borders, and new ways to spread images instantly.

breaks: The 1968 revolts had many separate causes, from Vietnam to Soviet rule, while the 2020 protests shared one focus: policing and racial injustice.

theme: Energy supply turned into a weapon

then.title: The 1973 oil crisis
then.hook: Empty highways on car-free Sundays and long lines at gas stations.
then.text: In October 1973, during the Yom Kippur War, Arab oil producers cut output and embargoed the United States and the Netherlands for supporting Israel. Oil prices roughly quadrupled within months. Several European countries banned Sunday driving.

now.title: Europe’s 2022 energy crisis
now.hook: Remember autumn 2022: thermostats turned down, shop windows dimmed, and dread opening the energy bill.
now.text: After invading Ukraine, Russia cut pipeline gas to Europe and halted Nord Stream 1 in September 2022. Wholesale gas prices rose to more than ten times pre-crisis levels. Governments capped bills, and EU countries agreed to cut gas use by 15%.

followed: Years of stagflation followed. Rich nations founded the International Energy Agency in 1974, built emergency oil stocks, and turned to smaller cars, nuclear power and new oil from the North Sea and Alaska.

next.title: A squeeze on battery metals
next.text: Around 2071, the choke point might be lithium, cobalt or rare earths for batteries and motors, with a dominant supplier cutting exports to win a political fight.
next.watch: Export controls on critical minerals, refining concentrated in one or two countries, and power grids leaning on a single foreign source.

breaks: In 2022 Europe also chose to cut its own Russian imports, and it replaced much of the lost gas with shipped liquefied gas within about a year.

then.title: The Fall of Saigon
then.hook: Helicopters lifting people off a Saigon rooftop as the Vietnam War ended.
then.text: On 30 April 1975, North Vietnamese tanks broke through the gates of the presidential palace and South Vietnam surrendered. In the final hours, US helicopters flew about 7,000 Americans and Vietnamese out of the city in Operation Frequent Wind.

now.title: The Fall of Kabul
now.hook: Remember August 2021: crowds running alongside a US military plane on Kabul airport’s runway.
now.text: The Taliban entered Kabul on 15 August 2021 as US troops were withdrawing, and President Ashraf Ghani fled. A chaotic airlift flew out more than 120,000 people. A suicide bombing at an airport gate killed about 170 Afghans and 13 US troops.

followed: Vietnam was formally reunified under communist rule in 1976. Cambodia and Laos also fell to communist forces in 1975, and hundreds of thousands of “boat people” fled Vietnam by sea.

next.title: Another great power’s rushed last flight
next.text: Around 2067, a major power might again fly its last people out of a capital after a long intervention, with the scramble broadcast live from drones and phones.
next.watch: Long foreign deployments losing support at home, fixed withdrawal deadlines, and local armies that depend on outside air power and contractors.

breaks: US combat troops had left Vietnam two years before Saigon fell to a conventional army, while Kabul fell to an insurgency before the US withdrawal was finished.

theme: Crushing inflation with sharply higher rates

then.title: The Volcker shock
then.hook: Interest rates near 20% and a Fed chair set on breaking inflation, whatever the cost.
then.text: Fed chair Paul Volcker pushed short-term interest rates to about 20% in 1980 to break inflation that peaked near 15%. Angry home builders mailed him pieces of lumber. Two recessions followed, and unemployment hit 10.8% in 1982.

now.title: The great rate hikes of 2022
now.hook: Remember 2022: grocery prices jumping every week and mortgage rates doubling within a year.
now.text: With US inflation at 9.1% in June 2022, the Federal Reserve raised rates from near zero to over 4% by December, including four three-quarter-point hikes in a row. The European Central Bank and Bank of England also raised rates quickly.

followed: US inflation fell to about 3% by 1983 and stayed lower for decades. Mexico said in 1982 it could not pay its debts, starting a Latin American debt crisis.

next.title: Another painful fight against inflation
next.text: Around 2064, a central bank might again choose between tolerating inflation driven by debt, aging or climate costs and causing a recession to stop it.
next.watch: Government debt growing faster than economies, political pressure on central banks to keep rates low, and inflation stuck above target for years.

breaks: Volcker’s rates neared 20% and came with deep recessions, while the 2022 hikes topped out near 5.5% and inflation eased without a 1980s-style slump.

theme: A nuclear disaster shakes faith in atomic power

then.title: The Chernobyl disaster
then.hook: A Soviet reactor explodes, and Sweden detects the radiation before Moscow admits anything.
then.text: On 26 April 1986, reactor No. 4 at Chernobyl exploded during a safety test. About 49,000 people in nearby Pripyat were evacuated the next day. Thirty-one people died in the short term, and fallout spread across Europe.

now.title: The Fukushima nuclear disaster
now.hook: Remember March 2011: a tsunami sweeping over Japan, then TV footage of reactor buildings exploding.
now.text: On 11 March 2011, a magnitude 9.0 earthquake sent a tsunami about 14 meters high over the Fukushima Daiichi plant. Three reactors melted down and more than 150,000 people were evacuated. Germany soon decided to close all its nuclear plants.

followed: The disaster pushed Mikhail Gorbachev toward more openness, or glasnost, and slowed nuclear building worldwide. Gorbachev later called Chernobyl perhaps the real cause of the Soviet collapse.

next.title: Nuclear fears return with new reactors
next.text: Around 2036, a serious accident could strike a reactor caught in a war zone or one of the new small reactors built to power data centers.
next.watch: Reactors on front lines like Zaporizhzhia, old plants run past their design life, and a rush to build small reactors quickly.

breaks: Chernobyl was caused by a flawed reactor and a botched test inside a secretive state, while Fukushima was triggered by a tsunami that overwhelmed its defenses.

theme: Mass protests over political freedoms under Beijing

then.title: The Tiananmen Square protests
then.hook: A lone man standing in front of a column of tanks in Beijing.
then.text: After reformer Hu Yaobang died in April 1989, students occupied Beijing’s Tiananmen Square for seven weeks, calling for political reform and press freedom. On the night of 3-4 June, troops cleared the area by force. The government put the death toll near 300; other estimates are far higher.

now.title: The Hong Kong protests
now.hook: Remember summer 2019: Hong Kong streets filled with black-clad marchers holding umbrellas against tear gas.
now.text: Protests began in June 2019 against a bill allowing extradition to mainland China. Organizers said about 2 million marched on 16 June; police gave lower figures. The bill was withdrawn in October, and in 2020 Beijing enacted a national security law for the city.

followed: Beijing said the crackdown ensured stability, while Western governments imposed sanctions, including an EU arms embargo. Deng Xiaoping relaunched market reforms in 1992, and the events remain censored in mainland China.

next.title: New protest tools meet new controls
next.text: Around 2049, the 100th anniversary of the People’s Republic, a generation raised online might find new ways to press demands, and authorities new ways to respond.
next.watch: The approach of 2047, when Hong Kong’s 50-year “one country, two systems” guarantee ends, and job prospects for young graduates.

breaks: Hong Kong kept its own laws and police under “one country, two systems”, and its protests wound down amid arrests, pandemic rules and a new security law, without the army.

theme: A new technology reaches everyone at once

then.title: The Netscape Navigator browser
then.hook: The browser that took millions of people onto the World Wide Web for the first time.
then.text: Released in December 1994 by a startup co-founded by Marc Andreessen, Netscape Navigator made the web easy for ordinary people to browse. Within months it was the most-used browser in the world.

now.title: The launch of ChatGPT
now.hook: Remember December 2022: everyone sharing screenshots of a chatbot writing poems, essays and computer code.
now.text: OpenAI released ChatGPT on 30 November 2022 as a free research preview. It passed 1 million users in five days and an estimated 100 million in about two months, the fastest growth yet seen for a consumer app.

followed: Netscape’s 1995 stock debut helped set off the dot-com boom. Microsoft bundled Internet Explorer with Windows, won the “browser war” and faced a US antitrust case, and AOL bought Netscape in 1999.

next.title: The next technology everyone adopts overnight
next.text: Around 2050, another tool might reach hundreds of millions within weeks, perhaps brain-computer interfaces or household robots, setting off its own boom, bust and fight over who controls it.
next.watch: Lab demos that suddenly become cheap consumer products, user records broken in days, and investors rushing into a single new category.

breaks: The web Netscape opened ran on open, shared standards, while the leading AI models cost vast sums to build and are controlled by a handful of firms.

theme: Science crosses a line in making life

then.title: Dolly the cloned sheep
then.hook: A Scottish sheep named Dolly that made the world ask whether humans would be cloned next.
then.text: Born at the Roslin Institute in July 1996 and unveiled in February 1997, Dolly was the first mammal cloned from an adult cell. She was the only lamb from 277 attempts, and her birth set off a global debate about human cloning.

now.title: The first gene-edited babies
now.hook: Remember November 2018: a Chinese scientist announcing on YouTube that gene-edited twin girls had been born.
now.text: Scientist He Jiankui said he had used CRISPR to edit the CCR5 gene in twin girls’ embryos, aiming to make them resistant to HIV. Scientists worldwide condemned the work. In 2019 a Chinese court sentenced him to three years in prison.

followed: Dozens of countries banned human reproductive cloning, and the UN adopted a non-binding declaration against it in 2005. In 2006, Japan’s Shinya Yamanaka found how to reprogram adult cells into stem cells without using embryos.

next.title: Babies from lab-grown eggs and sperm
next.text: Around 2040, a clinic might announce a baby made from eggs or sperm grown from skin cells, reigniting the debate Dolly began.
next.watch: Lab-grown human eggs and sperm, embryo screening sold for traits, and countries with loose rules on reproductive technology.

breaks: Dolly was a sheep made by a team that published its work openly, while He secretly edited human embryos, making heritable changes in real children.
older: Louise Brown, the first IVF baby, 1978

theme: A machine beats the best human player

then.title: Deep Blue beats Kasparov
then.hook: The world chess champion walking away from the board, beaten by an IBM computer.
then.text: In May 1997, IBM’s Deep Blue beat world champion Garry Kasparov 3½ to 2½ in a six-game rematch in New York. It searched about 200 million positions per second. Kasparov suggested humans had helped the machine; IBM denied it.

now.title: AlphaGo beats Lee Sedol
now.hook: Remember March 2016: Google’s AlphaGo beating Go champion Lee Sedol, years before experts expected.
now.text: In March 2016, Google DeepMind’s AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, one of the world’s top Go players, 4 to 1 in Seoul. Its move 37 in game two stunned professionals. Many experts had expected this milestone to be a decade away.

followed: Chess engines soon outplayed every human, and players began training with them. Kasparov promoted human-computer teams, and IBM moved on to Watson, which won the TV quiz show Jeopardy! in 2011.

next.title: AI outthinks humans at discovery
next.text: Around 2035, a machine might beat the best humans at something once seen as deeply creative, perhaps solving a famous open problem in mathematics or designing a working medicine largely on its own.
next.watch: AI systems producing original mathematical proofs, running lab experiments without human direction, and top experts in a field conceding defeat.

breaks: Deep Blue won through brute-force search hand-tuned by experts, while AlphaGo learned much of its play from data and self-play, a method that spread far beyond games.

then.title: The Y2K millennium bug
then.hook: Stockpiled water and fears that planes, banks and power grids would fail at midnight.
then.text: Old software stored years as two digits, so 2000 could be read as 1900 and break systems. Governments and companies spent an estimated $300 billion or more on fixes. When midnight came on 1 January 2000, only minor glitches were reported.

now.title: The CrowdStrike global IT outage
now.hook: Remember 19 July 2024: blue screens on airport departure boards and handwritten boarding passes.
now.text: A faulty CrowdStrike security update crashed about 8.5 million Windows computers within hours. Airlines grounded flights, hospitals postponed procedures and some broadcasters went off air. Delta alone canceled about 7,000 flights over five days.

followed: Y2K became a byword for overblown fear, though many engineers said the quiet midnight proved the fixes had worked. Within months the dot-com bubble burst.

next.title: One bad update stops the world
next.text: Around 2049, a single faulty update or hidden bug might freeze far more critical systems, from power grids to fleets of self-driving cars, across the world in minutes.
next.watch: The Year 2038 problem, when older 32-bit Unix clocks overflow, and essential services relying on the same few software vendors.

breaks: Y2K was a known deadline that years of work largely defused, while the CrowdStrike crash came without warning from one company’s routine update.

then.title: The dot-com crash
then.hook: Sock puppet mascots, Super Bowl ads, and internet startups that vanished almost overnight.
then.text: The tech-heavy Nasdaq index peaked in March 2000, then lost about 78% by October 2002. Hundreds of internet startups with little revenue folded, including Pets.com, which shut down nine months after its stock debut.

now.title: The crypto crash and FTX collapse
now.hook: Remember November 2022: FTX, the crypto exchange with its name on an arena, collapsing within days.
now.text: Crypto markets lost about $2 trillion from their late-2021 peak, and Bitcoin fell from about $69,000 to below $16,000. In November 2022 the FTX exchange collapsed, with about $8 billion in customer money missing. Founder Sam Bankman-Fried was later convicted of fraud.

followed: Survivors such as Amazon and eBay grew into giants, and Google went public in 2004. Many economists argue the low interest rates after the crash helped feed the housing bubble that burst in 2008.

next.title: A new technology bubble bursts
next.text: Around 2044, a fresh frenzy might build around a promising technology, perhaps quantum computing, space or some invention not yet named, then burst when profits come more slowly than promised.
next.watch: Company values far ahead of revenue, first-time investors piling in through phone apps, and celebrities promoting assets they are paid to endorse.

breaks: The dot-com bubble funded the internet, which went on to reshape daily life, while crypto’s lasting uses are still debated.

theme: A sudden grid collapse darkens millions

then.title: The Northeast blackout of 2003
then.hook: New Yorkers walking home across bridges in the heat as the city’s lights went out.
then.text: On 14 August 2003, power lines sagging into trees in Ohio and a failed alarm system set off a cascade. About 55 million people in eight US states and Ontario lost power, some for days. Subways stopped and traffic lights went dark.

now.title: The Iberian blackout
now.hook: Remember 28 April 2025: dead traffic lights, stalled trains and battery radios across Spain and Portugal.
now.text: On 28 April 2025, at 12:33 Spanish time, the grids of Spain and Portugal collapsed within seconds. Trains stalled, phone networks faltered and tens of millions lost power until late that night or the next morning. Investigators traced it to a chain of voltage surges that tripped power plants.

followed: A US-Canada task force blamed overgrown trees, failed alarms and operator errors at an Ohio utility. The Energy Policy Act of 2005 then made grid reliability rules mandatory across North America.

next.title: A more electric world goes dark
next.text: Around 2047, with cars, heating and cooking running on electricity, a cyberattack, solar storm or control failure might black out a whole country and freeze daily life.
next.watch: How grids keep voltage stable as power sources change, cyberattacks on utilities, strong solar storms, and thin links between national grids.

breaks: In 2003 failures built up over hours on part of a vast continental grid, while in 2025 two whole countries, weakly linked to Europe, collapsed in seconds.
